questions.stem: How is a look-out kept, according to Rule 5 and the STCW principles?
options: By AIS, which replaces the need to look
By sight, by hearing and by all available means, at all times
By radar only in restricted visibility
By sight only in daylight and by radar at night
questions.explanation: The look-out is kept by sight, hearing and all available means, at all times. Radar and AIS support the look-out, they do not replace eyes and ears, and the look-out is not limited to restricted visibility.

questions.stem: Which list gives the purposes of a look-out?
options: Continuous vigilance, full appraisal of the situation and risk of collision, stranding and other dangers, and detecting ships or aircraft in distress, shipwrecked persons, wrecks and debris
Logging the weather, steering the ship and checking the engine room
Reporting only other ships' lights and nothing else
Keeping the master informed about cargo and passenger numbers
questions.explanation: The purposes are vigilance, appraisal of collision, stranding and other dangers, and detecting distress, wrecks and debris. The other lists describe other jobs or only part of the picture.

questions.stem: A look-out sees a light, hears a sound signal and notices a floating log. What should be reported?
options: Only the light, because it is a vessel
Only things that look dangerous
Only objects within one mile
Every one of them, with its approximate bearing in degrees or points
questions.explanation: A look-out reports every light, shape, sound signal and object with an approximate bearing in degrees or points. Judging what is important is for the officer once the information reaches the bridge.

questions.stem: When is the helmsperson considered to be the look-out while steering?
options: Never, in any ship
Whenever the vessel is under 500 GT
Only in a small ship that gives an unobstructed all-round view from the steering position
Whenever the autopilot is off
questions.explanation: The principles treat the duties as separate and make an exception only for small ships with an unobstructed all-round view at the steering position. Size alone (500 GT) is not the test.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions allows an officer to be the sole look-out?
options: Daylight, with no need for a prior assessment
Daylight, careful assessment of the situation, and help immediately available on the bridge
Good visibility at any hour, with the radar on
Night, with a clear radar picture and the autopilot on
questions.explanation: All three conditions must hold: daylight, a careful assessment (weather, visibility, traffic, dangers) and immediate help. Night does not qualify and assessment cannot be skipped.

questions.stem: Roughly how long can full dark adaptation of the eyes take, and what can undo it?
options: As long as about 30 minutes; a brief exposure to bright light can undo it
About 30 seconds; it cannot be undone
About 2 hours; only sleep undoes it
About 5 minutes; nothing can undo it
questions.explanation: Research gives as long as 30 minutes for full adaptation, with much of the gain in the first few minutes, and shows that brief bright light can reverse it. This is a study-aid figure to confirm with your instructor.

questions.stem: At night you can just make out a faint light when looking straight at it, and it vanishes. What helps?
options: Stare at it without blinking
Switch on the deck floodlights
Look at the radar screen for a few seconds first
Look 5 to 10 degrees to one side of it
questions.explanation: The centre of the eye is poor in the dark, so look slightly to one side. Floodlights and a bright screen both damage night vision.

questions.stem: Using the window wiper method, a look-out scans a 150-degree window in 10-degree sectors, 4 seconds in each. How long does one pass across take, and how long does across and back take?
options: 150 seconds across, 300 seconds across and back
15 seconds across, 30 seconds across and back
60 seconds across, 120 seconds across and back
40 seconds across, 80 seconds across and back
questions.explanation: 150 ÷ 10 = 15 sectors, and 15 × 4 = 60 seconds one way, so 120 seconds there and back. The other answers use the wrong number of sectors or the wrong time per sector.

questions.stem: Which statement about additional look-outs matches the guidance used in this course?
options: It says radar makes additional look-outs unnecessary
It advises against the officer being the sole look-out in darkness and supports additional look-outs in restricted visibility
It requires every vessel to carry six look-outs in fog
It says additional look-outs are only needed above 1,000 GT
questions.explanation: UK guidance (MGN 137), used as supporting context, advises against sole look-out in darkness and for extra look-outs in restricted visibility. It sets no number of six, no 1,000 GT line and does not treat radar as a substitute. It is not Canadian law.

questions.stem: You are steering a 20 m vessel from a wheelhouse where the pillars block your view astern and to port. The officer says "You are the look-out too." Which response is most accurate?
options: The helmsperson is not the look-out while steering unless the steering position gives an unobstructed all-round view, so another look-out is needed
That is fine because the vessel is small
That is fine in daylight
That is fine if the radar has a guard zone set
questions.explanation: The exception needs an unobstructed all-round view from the steering position. Small size, daylight or a radar guard zone do not meet that condition.
